entries.what_happened: Two manuscripts from the openai/math release are matched. (1) “The Kakeya maximal conjecture in three dimensions” (dated 23 September 2026) claims that for every ε > 0 and 0 < δ < 1, the radius-δ tube maximal operator K_δ f(ω) = sup over centres a of the average of |f| over the unit tube T_δ(a, ω) satisfies ‖K_δ f‖_{L³(S²)} ≤ C_ε δ^{-ε} ‖f‖_{L³(ℝ³)} for all f in L³(ℝ³). The main theorem matches the abstract. The proof is a contradiction argument on a critical exponent (the proposition “Vanishing at the maximal endpoint”, in the closing section), followed by a reduction from the critical inequality to the maximal bound. The manuscript also states Nikodym maximal estimates on ℝ³ and on local constant-curvature 3-manifolds, and a local curved Kakeya estimate for one fixed translation-invariant phase. It states no Hausdorff or Minkowski dimension conclusion of its own. (2) “Every four-dimensional Kakeya set has full Hausdorff dimension” (dated 24 September 2026) claims in its main theorem that if K ⊂ ℝ⁴ contains, for every e ∈ S³, a segment {a_e + te : 0 ≤ t ≤ 1} ⊂ K, then dim_H K = 4. No measurability, compactness or regularity is assumed on K or on the family of segments. Its consequences section adds: a bounded such K has lower and upper Minkowski dimension 4; every such K has packing dimension 4; every Kakeya set in ℝᵈ with d ≥ 4 has Hausdorff dimension at least 4, by projection onto a 4-dimensional subspace; if a set E contains a segment in every direction of a set D ⊂ ℝP³, then dim_H E ≥ 1 + dim_H D; and Nikodym sets and fixed-phase curved Kakeya sets in dimension 4 have full dimension.
entries.delivers: For part (a) of the list's problem at n = 4, the second manuscript gives exactly the list's claim: a set in ℝ⁴ containing a unit segment in every direction has Hausdorff dimension 4. Its statement of the problem matches the list's, and it assumes no compactness or measurability, as the list requires. For part (b) at n = 4, it gives Minkowski dimension 4 only for bounded sets, where lower and upper Minkowski dimension are both 4. The list gives no convention for unbounded sets, and the manuscript does not treat them beyond the packing-dimension statement. So (b) is settled in ℝ⁴ for bounded sets only. For n = 3, the first manuscript gives a quantitative maximal estimate with δ^{-ε} loss at L³ → L³. The list treats n = 3 as already settled by Wang and Zahl (2025), so this is a stronger maximal form in that dimension and not a new set-dimension statement. For n ≥ 5, the second manuscript gives only the lower bound 4 for Hausdorff dimension, not n, and no Minkowski statement.
entries.remains: (a) For every n ≥ 5, both parts: the list's full conjecture is open, and the manuscript proves only Hausdorff dimension at least 4 there. (b) In ℝ⁴, the Minkowski dimension of unbounded Kakeya sets, which the list leaves without a convention. (c) For n = 3, the list's two parts were already settled by Wang and Zahl (2025), so nothing in the list's wording is new. The maximal estimate in ℝ³ is a separate, stronger statement that the list does not ask for. The first manuscript proves it only at p = 3 on ℝ³; other exponents appear only in the Nikodym corollary.
entries.direction: proves the conjecture for n = 4 (Hausdorff dimension; Minkowski for bounded sets); proves the maximal form for n = 3 (set case already settled); lower bound 4 for n ≥ 5
entries.conditional_on: First manuscript: the main proof uses the Guth–Wang–Zahl convex-clustering set estimate (arXiv:2601.14411, Theorem 1.1) as a black box, applied under its density threshold λ ≥ δ^η. The manuscript's added content is keeping the density power λ³. Wang–Zahl's theorem (arXiv:2502.17655) gives only λ^{K(ε)}. The proof also uses Ren–Wang's planar Furstenberg estimate (arXiv:2308.08819) in Wang–Wu's shaded form (arXiv:2411.08871, Theorem 0.6), and the Bennett–Carbery–Tao and Guth multilinear Kakeya theorems. The Nikodym and curved corollaries rely on Gao–Liu–Xi's transfer theorems (arXiv:2503.11574). A separate OpenAI preprint, “Elliptic capacity propagation and Fourier restriction to the sphere”, is cited as an independent alternative route, not as a dependency. Second manuscript: the three-dimensional estimate in its reduction is the weighted full-time plank bound cited as [ThreeDimensional], Lemma 2.3. That is the sibling OpenAI manuscript above, whose proof rests on the Guth–Wang–Zahl theorem. The argument also uses Carbery–Valdimarsson's multilinear Kakeya theorem, Wang–Zahl's restricted triple dot-product theorem (JAMS 2026), Orponen–de Saxcé–Shmerkin's Theorem 1.5 (arXiv:2309.03068), and the Sudakov–Szemerédi–Vu and Tao–Vu graph lemma, which the manuscript proves in its own form. Its consequences section depends on Keleti–Máthé (arXiv:2203.15731) for direction sets and line extension, on Gao–Liu–Xi (Theorem 1.5, Theorem 1.12, Corollary 4.2) for Nikodym and curved statements, and on Nadjimzadah's lifting preprint (arXiv:2609.06299, v1, September 2026, Theorem 1.3) for the three-dimensional quadratic curved corollary.
entries.doubts: First manuscript: the text flags no step as sketched or conjectural, and the abstract agrees with the main theorem. The new density exponent λ³ is the central claim. It is obtained in the closing section by a long contradiction argument over a stationary construction spread across roughly sections 10 to 70. I read the introduction, the closing section, the inputs section and the consequences section, but did not verify the intermediate chain. The Nikodym and curved corollaries are obtained by invoking Gao–Liu–Xi's transfers, and the reduction is given in a few sentences; the manifold constants depend on a compact straightening chart. Second manuscript: no step is flagged as sketched, and the abstract agrees with the main theorem. The main theorem depends on a sibling manuscript from the same family (the three-dimensional lemma) and on a 2026 preprint for the set estimate. I read the introduction, the reduction theorem at the start of the reduction section, the start of the retained-edge section, and the completion proof, but not the propositions in between. In the consequences section the curved corollary's normal form is attributed to “their proof” of Gao–Liu–Xi rather than to a stated result, and the Nikodym corollary takes its Kakeya lower bound from Gao–Liu–Xi's Theorem 1.5 without new argument. The introduction says the consequences use transfer results “with their distinct hypotheses stated there”.
